content: The following is a professional interpretation of the provided data: 1. Prognostic Properties of IADPSG Criteria for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) in Predicting Large-for-Gestational-Age (LGA) Births: The analysis included four cohort studies with a total of 28,755 pregnancies. The diagnostic test used was a 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) applying IADPSG cut-offs, performed universally at 24–28 weeks of gestation. The clinical outcome assessed was the occurrence of LGA births. The sensitivity of the test was 91% (95% CI: 72–110), and the specificity was 83.2% (95% CI: 24–33). There was significant heterogeneity across studies, with better results observed in the HAPO study, which originally generated the IADPSG criteria. Complications and costs were not reported in the studies. 2. Prognostic Properties of 1999 WHO Criteria for GDM in Predicting Pre-eclampsia: Three cohort studies involving 26,677 pregnancies were analyzed. The diagnostic test was a 75g OGTT applying the 1999 WHO cut-offs, performed universally at 24–28 weeks of gestation. The clinical outcome was the development of pre-eclampsia during pregnancy. The sensitivity of the test was 1.1% (95% CI: 6–8), and the specificity was 860 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 838–880). The quality of evidence was rated as high, with no serious limitations, inconsistency, or indirectness. Complications and costs were not reported. 3. Prognostic Properties of IADPSG Criteria for GDM in Predicting Pre-eclampsia: Three cohort studies with 35,052 pregnancies were included. The diagnostic test was a 75g OGTT applying IADPSG cut-offs, performed universally at 24–28 weeks of gestation. The clinical outcome was the development of pre-eclampsia. The sensitivity of the test was 12% (95% CI: 11–13), and the specificity was 796 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 777–816). There was moderate quality of evidence due to some inconsistency across studies. Complications and costs were not reported. 4. Prognostic Properties of 1999 WHO Criteria for GDM in Predicting Cesarean Section: Four cohort studies involving 30,045 pregnancies were analyzed. The diagnostic test was a 75g OGTT applying the 1999 WHO cut-offs, performed universally at 24–28 weeks of gestation. The clinical outcome was the occurrence of cesarean section. The sensitivity of the test was 1.2% (95% CI: 18–33), and the specificity was 715 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 677–754). The quality of evidence was moderate, with some serious limitations and inconsistency. Complications and costs were not reported. 5. Prognostic Properties of IADPSG Criteria for GDM in Predicting Cesarean Section: Three cohort studies with 33,788 pregnancies were included. The diagnostic test was a 75g OGTT applying IADPSG cut-offs, performed universally at 24–28 weeks of gestation. The clinical outcome was the occurrence of cesarean section. The sensitivity of the test was 1.8% (95% CI: 36.9–120), and the specificity was 117 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 77–185). The quality of evidence was low due to serious limitations and inconsistency. Complications and costs were not reported. 6. GRADE Evaluation of Universal Screening for GDM Using WHO Criteria: Universal screening for GDM using WHO criteria was compared to no screening in pregnant women from the general population. The intervention involved OGTT with specific treatment for women diagnosed with GDM. The outcomes assessed included adverse perinatal and maternal outcomes. The quality of evidence was very low due to serious limitations and indirectness. The absolute risk reduction (ARR) was 5 fewer per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 4–7). 7. GRADE Evaluation of Universal Screening for GDM Using IADPSG Criteria: Universal screening for GDM using IADPSG criteria was compared to no screening in pregnant women from the general population. The intervention involved OGTT with specific treatment for women diagnosed with GDM. The outcomes assessed included adverse perinatal and maternal outcomes. The quality of evidence was very low due to serious limitations, inconsistency, and indirectness. The ARR was 9 fewer per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 5–13). 8. Key Observations: Evidence from simulation models was used when direct evidence was unavailable. The absolute effect of GDM screening was highly dependent on the prevalence of GDM in the population and the sensitivity of the model. Better results were observed in the HAPO study population, which generated the IADPSG criteria. However, heterogeneity among observational studies was noted. This analysis highlights the varying quality of evidence and the need for further research to assess the effectiveness of GDM screening criteria in improving maternal and perinatal outcomes.
